title: Single-coordinate chains between flat quasi-finite affine-space charts
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-algebraic-closure], $d\geq0$, and $X$ a separated [def-weil-proper-morphism] finite-type $k$-scheme pure of dimension $d$ [def-weil-pure-dimension] [def-pc-scheme], [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. Suppose $X$ is Cohen–Macaulay, meaning that every local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ has depth equal to its Krull dimension [def-weil-pbc-depth], [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring]. Let $u,v:X\to\mathbf A^d_k$ be quasi-finite flat $k$-morphisms [def-sbc-affine-space], [pqf-def-quasifinite], [def-weil-flat-morphism]. For every closed point $x\in X$ [def-weil-closed-points] there are an open neighbourhood $U$ of $x$, an integer $r\geq0$, and quasi-finite flat $k$-morphisms $w_0,\ldots,w_r:U\to\mathbf A^d_k$ with $w_0=u|_U$, $w_r=v|_U$, such that each consecutive pair has all but at most one of its $d$ coordinate functions equal. For $d=0$ one may take $r=0$.

source.place: XVIII Lemmas 2.5–2.6, pp. 551–552; 2.5 uses prime avoidance and regular systems of parameters in Cohen–Macaulay local rings. No Stacks tag located for this chain-of-charts assertion.

proof.text: For $d=0$, $\mathbf A^0_k=\operatorname{Spec}k$ and both maps are the structure morphism; take $U=X$ and $r=0$. Henceforth let $d>0$ and fix the given closed point $x$. The closed-point residue-field lemma identifies $\kappa(x)$ with $k$. Put $A=\mathcal O_{X,x}$ and $\mathfrak m=\mathfrak m_x$, and center the two tuples: $\alpha_i=(u_i)_x-u_i(x)$ and $\beta_i=(v_i)_x-v_i(x)$. Apply the parameter-chart germ criterion to the actual coordinate sections of $u$ and $v$: since they are flat and quasi-finite, it gives that $A$ is Noetherian of dimension $d$ and that both centered tuples generate ideals with radical $\mathfrak m$. The Cohen–Macaulay hypothesis on $A$ is exactly the hypothesis on the stalk of $X$ at $x$.

source.place: XVIII 2.6, first proof paragraph and centering in the second paragraph, p. 552

proof.text: Prove the following local assertion by induction on $e$: in every nonzero Noetherian local ring $(B,\mathfrak n)$ of finite dimension $e$ with $\operatorname{depth}(B)\ge e$ (the Cohen–Macaulay condition used in this induction), any two ordered systems of parameters can be connected by a finite chain of ordered systems of parameters, changing at most one entry at each step. Here a system of parameters means an $e$-tuple in $\mathfrak n$ whose quotient has dimension zero, equivalently whose generated ideal has radical $\mathfrak n$. For $e=0$ both tuples are empty; for $e=1$ use the two given tuples as one edge (or no edge if equal). Suppose $e\ge2$ and assume the assertion for all such rings of dimension $e-1$. Denote the two tuples by $p=(p_1,\ldots,p_e)$ and $q=(q_1,\ldots,q_e)$.

Since $\dim B/(p)=\dim B/(q)=0$, the dimension-drop regular-sequence lemma with $c=e$ makes $p$ and $q$ regular sequences. Their first elements $p_1,q_1$ are therefore nonzerodivisors. The Cohen–Macaulay quotient lemma gives that $B/(p_1)$ and $B/(q_1)$ are nonzero Noetherian Cohen–Macaulay local rings of dimension $e-1$.

source.place: XVIII 2.5, use of the Cohen–Macaulay quotients by the first parameters; Stacks 02JN

proof.text: Choose a common element $z\in\mathfrak n$ which is a nonzerodivisor on all three rings $B$, $B/(p_1)$ and $B/(q_1)$. Here is the complete avoidance argument. Each of these rings has positive depth, so its maximal ideal cannot be an associated prime: a nonzero element killed by the whole maximal ideal would be killed by the first element of a positive-length regular sequence, contradicting injectivity. Each ring has finitely many associated primes. Pull the two quotient rings' associated primes back to $B$ and add the associated primes of $B$; all are prime ideals strictly smaller than $\mathfrak n$. By prime avoidance, $\mathfrak n$ has an element $z$ outside this finite union. The zero-divisor/associated-prime lemma in each of the three rings says precisely that these three multiplications by $z$ are injective. The sets can be handled as a finite family; if it is empty any element outside the empty union works. Including the associated primes of $B$ explicitly ensures that $B/(z)$ is a valid Cohen–Macaulay quotient for the middle induction below.

The pairs $(p_1,z)$ and $(q_1,z)$ are regular sequences by their injectivity just proved: both entries lie in $\mathfrak n$, so their generated ideals are proper and the final quotients are nonzero. The same observation applies to every subsequent tuple of lifts in $\mathfrak n$. Apply the Cohen–Macaulay quotient lemma twice to see that $B/(p_1,z)$ and $B/(q_1,z)$ are Cohen–Macaulay of dimension $e-2$. Their depth definition supplies regular sequences of length $e-2$ in their maximal ideals (for $e=2$ these are empty); choose lifts $a_3,\ldots,a_e$ and $b_3,\ldots,b_e$ in $\mathfrak n$. Repeated applications of the same quotient lemma to these sequences make the final quotients zero-dimensional. Thus $a=(p_1,z,a_3,\ldots,a_e)$ and $b=(q_1,z,b_3,\ldots,b_e)$ are systems of parameters. Also $B/(z)$ is Cohen–Macaulay of dimension $e-1$, since $z$ was chosen regular on $B$. For $e-2>0$, a supremum of lengths at least $e-2$ supplies a sequence of length at least $e-2$; truncate it to length $e-2$. Otherwise every length would be at most $e-3$. This uses only the lower bound on depth supplied by the quotient lemma, not an uncited depth-versus-dimension theorem.

source.place: XVIII 2.5, completing the pairs to the tuples a and b; Stacks 02JN

proof.text: By the Cohen–Macaulay quotient lemma, the three rings $B/(p_1)$, $B/(z)$ and $B/(q_1)$ satisfy the induction hypotheses in dimension $e-1$. Apply the induction hypothesis in $B/(p_1)$ to the tails of $p$ and $a$, in $B/(z)$ to the tuples obtained from $a$ and $b$ by deleting their second entry, and in $B/(q_1)$ to the tails of $b$ and $q$. These are systems of parameters in the respective $(e-1)$-dimensional rings because their final quotients are the zero-dimensional quotients by the full tuples. Lift each quotient chain with the omitted entry held fixed in its original coordinate position. More explicitly, start with the prescribed initial tuple upstairs; at each quotient edge change only the affected coordinate, choosing any lift of its new entry. At the final tuple each coordinate differs from its prescribed endpoint by a multiple of the fixed entry. Correct these coordinates one at a time. Each such correction leaves the ideal generated together with the fixed entry unchanged, so every tuple remains a system of parameters. This supplies exact endpoints upstairs, rather than endpoints only modulo the fixed entry. Concatenate the three lifted chains to obtain $p\rightsquigarrow a\rightsquigarrow b\rightsquigarrow q$. This finishes the induction. Apply its result to $A,\alpha,\beta$ from Step 1.

source.place: XVIII 2.5, three applications of the induction hypothesis; explicit lifting of quotient chains

proof.text: Realize the resulting finite chain of tuples in $\mathfrak m$ as functions near $x$. For each distinct germ occurring in the chain choose a representative section once, and intersect their finitely many neighbourhoods. The stalk description allows a further finite shrink so that the first and last tuple representatives equal the actual sections $u_i-u_i(x)$ and $v_i-v_i(x)$. Choosing one representative for each germ makes all equal adjacent coordinates equal as sections. Add at the beginning the explicit tuples $u-(u_1(x),\ldots,u_j(x),0,\ldots,0)$ for $j=0,\ldots,d$, and at the end the reverse analogous sequence for $v$. Consecutive tuples change at most one coordinate. Every centered germ tuple in a translation sequence equals $\alpha$ or $\beta$, and every tuple in the middle sequence is a system of parameters. The parameter-chart germ criterion, applied separately to these finitely many prescribed representative tuples, gives affine neighbourhoods on which each corresponding map is quasi-finite and flat. Choose an affine neighbourhood $U$ of $x$ inside their finite intersection. Flatness persists because the source stalks are unchanged on an open subscheme; fibre isolation persists on an open subset. Apply the affine-pairs characterization of local finite type to the structure map $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ and the affine open $U$: its section ring is a finitely generated $k$-algebra. On this affine $U$, each map to $\mathbf A^d_k$ is of finite type: a finite set of $k$-algebra generators of $\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)$ also generates it over the coordinate-polynomial algebra. The single affine source and target give the finite affine cover in the finite-type definition. Hence the maps are quasi-finite in the stated, finite-type sense. Enumerate this finite concatenation as $w_0,\ldots,w_r$. Its exact endpoints are $u|_U$ and $v|_U$, as required.

source.place: XVIII 2.6, realization of germs, common shrinking, and the explicit centering chains, p. 552; Stacks 01T2 for finite type on arbitrary affine pairs

split_report.summary: Read SGA XVIII 2.5–2.6 and wrote the local-ring induction inside this item, reusing existing Cohen–Macaulay quotient, regular-sequence, associated-prime and prime-avoidance tools. Added only the separate germ criterion implicit in SGA 2.6. Made the pivot regular also on the original ring, explained parameter completions and exact lifting endpoints, and used a finite common shrinking for the actual coordinate representatives. Clarified that the given morphisms are over k, as intended by SGA; without this the d=0 clause is false for two distinct automorphisms of Spec k. The separatedness hypothesis cites the separatedness definition carried by def-weil-proper-morphism.

lean.statement: theorem exists_flat_coordinate_chain {k : Type u} [Field k] [IsAlgClosed k] (d : ℕ) (X : Scheme.{u}) [X.Over (Spec (CommRingCat.of k))] [IsSeparated (X ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of k))] [LocallyOfFiniteType (X ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of k))] [QuasiCompact (X ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of k))] (hpure : X.IsPureDimension d) (hCM : ∀ y : X, (IsLocalRing.depth (R := X.presheaf.stalk y) (X.presheaf.stalk y) : WithBot ℕ∞) = ringKrullDim (X.presheaf.stalk y)) (f g : X ⟶ 𝔸(ULift.{u} (Fin d); Spec (CommRingCat.of k))) [f.IsOver (Spec (CommRingCat.of k))] [g.IsOver (Spec (CommRingCat.of k))] (hf : f.IsQuasiFinite) (hg : g.IsQuasiFinite) [Flat f] [Flat g] (x : X) (hx : x ∈ closedPoints X) : ∃ (U : X.Opens) (_hxU : x ∈ U) (r : ℕ) (w : Fin (r + 1) → (U.toScheme ⟶ 𝔸(ULift.{u} (Fin d); Spec (CommRingCat.of k)))), (∀ j, w j ≫ 𝔸(ULift.{u} (Fin d); Spec (CommRingCat.of k)) ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of k) = U.ι ≫ X ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of k)) ∧ (∀ j, (w j).IsQuasiFinite ∧ Flat (w j)) ∧ w 0 = U.ι ≫ f ∧ w (Fin.last r) = U.ι ≫ g ∧ (∀ j : Fin r, Set.Subsingleton {i : ULift.{u} (Fin d) | (w j.castSucc).appTop (AffineSpace.coord (Spec (CommRingCat.of k)) i) ≠ (w j.succ).appTop (AffineSpace.coord (Spec (CommRingCat.of k)) i)}) ∧ (d = 0 → r = 0)
